And that the bonds of lineage and tribe had to be cast aside was demonstrated when, on the battlefields of **Badr and Uḥud**, swords were crossed between father and son and between brother and brother. These, it says, are significant evidences of the creed they held dear.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes its comment on ayah 23 with a supplication worth carrying: *Yā Allah, bless us with the ability to follow them, and make Your love the dearest of everything in our sight, and make Your fear the most fear-worthy of everything with us.*

## Living it

**On migration.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the standing rules this ayah leaves behind:

1. When Hijrah from Makkah to Madīnah was made obligatory, it was not simply a matter of obligation — it was also a hallmark and symbol of being a Muslim: anyone who did not migrate then, despite having the ability, was not taken to be a Muslim. **This injunction was abrogated after the Conquest of Makkah.**
2. The basic injunction that remained operative: should there be a land where a person cannot comply with his religious obligations — such as praying and fasting in accordance with the injunctions of Allah — then migrating from there remains a duty (*farḍ*, obligatory) forever, on condition that he is capable of undertaking it. This is the first degree of compliance.
3. Compliance in the second degree: that one should leave every place where sin and disobedience have a dominant role in life. This remains *mustaḥabb* (recommended) forever. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refers the details to *Fatḥ al-Bārī*.)

**On the address itself.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the **generality of the words** tells all Muslims that love for Allah and His Messenger ﷺ is obligatory upon them in a special degree: the highest, the foremost — a degree that requires that no other bond or love for anyone or anything should ever prevail over it. Whoever fails to come up to that level of love becomes deserving of punishment from Allah. Let him, then, wait for it.

**A concrete sign.** Al-Bayḍāwī, as cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, adds one visible mark: the preservation and protection of the Sunnah (the Prophet's ﷺ way) and the Sharīʿah (the sacred law), and the rebuttal of and defence against those who oppose or malign them, is also an open sign of love for Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.

**A note from the surrounding stretch.** Among the points Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from ayat 19–23 is that **sin and disobedience spoil human reason**, so that one starts taking good as bad and bad as good — a hint released by the statement at the end of ayah 19, *And Allah does not lead the wrongdoing people to the right path*. It is counterbalanced in another verse: *If you fear Allah, He will provide you with a criterion* to distinguish between right and wrong (8:29). Obeying Allah and fearing Him gives polish and lustre to human reason, balance and poise to thinking, and a never-failing ability to distinguish between good and bad.

---

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ends its comment on ayah 24 with a second prayer: *May Allah bless us and bless all Muslims with love for Him and love for His Messenger ﷺ.*

passages.title: The lesson of Hunayn: numbers never win
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

Allah reminds the believers of a day when they were more numerous, better armed and more confident than they had ever been — and yet found themselves running.

Ayah 25 opens with Allah's help on many battlefields, then names one in particular: **the day of Hunayn**. Allah helped them there too, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out — but only after they had rejoiced in their own great numbers, found the wide earth closing in on them, and turned back in flight. Ayah 26 is the answer: Allah sent down His *sakīnah* on His Messenger ﷺ and on the believers, and sent down forces they did not see. Ayah 27 leaves a door standing open — even those defeated that day may yet be turned to in mercy, "and Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."

Ibn Jurayj reported from Mujahid that this was the first ayah of Barāʾah in which Allah reminds the believers of how He favoured and blessed them with victory in many battles alongside His Messenger ﷺ. And the point of the reminder, as Ibn Kathir draws it out, is that victory comes from Allah, "by His aid and decree, not because of their numbers or adequate supplies," whether the triumphs are few or many. Only a few remained with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that day, and Allah sent down His aid to him and to those few. Many a small group has overcome a larger one by Allah's leave, and Allah is ever with those who are patient.

## Why Hunayn, of all the battles

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the choice of this battle: so much of what happened at Hunayn unfolded unexpectedly and extraordinarily that thinking it through "makes one stronger in faith and bolder in deed."

Hunayn is about ten miles from Makkah — Ibn Kathir calls it a valley between the two cities. The battle took place in Shawwāl of the eighth year after the Hijrah, shortly after Makkah was conquered in Ramaḍān and its people, most of whom then embraced Islam, were set free.

The tribe of Thaqīf in Ṭāʾif — a branch of Hawāzin, a people known all over Arabia as big, brave, rich and warring — looked at the sudden strength of the Muslims and concluded that once the Muslims had settled down, their turn was coming. They decided to strike first. Under Mālik ibn ʿAwf they brought together every branch of Hawāzin from Makkah to Ṭāʾif; Ibn Kathir names alongside them Banū Jusham, Banū Saʿd ibn Bakr, some people of Banū Hilāl and others.

Two small branches, Banū Kaʿb and Banū Kilāb, did not approve. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records them saying that even if the forces of the whole world from East to West came together against Muhammad ﷺ, he would still overcome them all, and that they could not fight against the power of Allah. Allah, the commentary says, had blessed those two branches with some foresight. The rest all gave their pledges to fight.

Mālik ibn ʿAwf then made a decision that would cost his people everything: every participant was to bring his family and his valuables to the battlefield. His reasoning: if a man thought of bolting, the love of wife, children and property behind him would hold him back like shackles on his feet. As for their numbers, the historians differ: Ibn Ḥajar and others weigh the reports at twenty-four or twenty-eight thousand; others give four thousand. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān suggests both can be true — four thousand actual fighting men, and the larger figure once women and children are counted.

## What the Muslims brought — and what they said

Ibn Kathir gives ten thousand from the Muhājirīn, the Anṣār and various Arab tribes, and with them the *Ṭulaqāʾ* numbering two thousand — the Makkans who had embraced Islam when the city was conquered and whom he had set free. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing a narration of Imam Zuhrī, counts fourteen thousand in all: twelve thousand who had accompanied him for the conquest of Makkah, and the two thousand Makkan new Muslims. He appointed ʿAttāb ibn Asīd over Makkah and left Muʿādh ibn Jabal behind to teach the people Islam.

He needed weapons and war supplies, and the men who had them were the very Makkans who had just laid down their arms before him. Ṣafwān ibn Umayyah asked bluntly: did he mean to take this material from them by force, against their will? The Prophet ﷺ replied: no — a borrowing, guaranteed to be returned. Ṣafwān gave a hundred coats of mail; Nawfal ibn Ḥārith gave three thousand spears. Everything borrowed was later returned.

Setting out on Saturday the 6th of Shawwāl, he said that the next day, Allah willing, they would camp at Khaif Banī Kinānah — the very spot where the Quraysh of Makkah had once assembled to write down their pledge to excommunicate the Muslims.

Behind the fourteen thousand trailed another crowd — many men and women of Makkah who came out as spectators, their hearts excited with conflicting emotions. If the Muslims were defeated, here was their chance at revenge; if the Muslims won, they consoled themselves that they had lost nothing.

Shaibah ibn ʿUthmān was one of these spectators. His father had been killed at Badr by Ḥamzah and his uncle by ʿAlī, and his heart was full of anger. He walked with the Muslim forces for one purpose — to find his opportunity and strike the Prophet ﷺ. When he saw some Muslims running, he seized the moment and got close, only to find ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās guarding him on the right and Abū Sufyān ibn al-Ḥārith on the left. So he dashed to the rear, meaning to strike suddenly from behind. Right then the Prophet ﷺ looked at him and called him by name — "Shaibah, come here" — drew him close, put his blessed hand on his chest and prayed that Shayṭān be removed from him. When Shaibah raised his eyes, he said, the Prophet ﷺ had become dearer to him than his own eye and ear and life; he was sent off to fight, and staked his life fighting to the end. Afterwards the Prophet ﷺ told him what had been in his heart when he set off from Makkah. He had known.

Something similar, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, happened to Naḍr ibn Ḥārith, who came to Hunayn with the same intention and left as a valiant fighter for Islam.

And at Awṭās, Abū Burdah ibn Niyār found the Prophet ﷺ sitting under a tree with a stranger beside him. The Prophet ﷺ explained: he had been asleep when this man came, seized his sword, stood over his head and said, "O Muhammad, now tell me who can save you from me?" He answered, "Allah!" — and the sword fell from the man's hands. Abū Burdah asked leave to behead him. The Prophet ﷺ said only: *say no more; Allah is my Protector until my religion prevails over all others* — and let the man go without a single word of reproach.

## The words that were said, and the morning that followed

When Suhail ibn Ḥanẓalah brought news that the whole of Hawāzin had arrived with an array of war material, the Prophet ﷺ smiled and said: do not worry, all this material has come as spoils for the Muslims.

This was the first time the Muslims had marched out fourteen thousand strong, with far more war material than they had ever had; and they had the experience of Badr and Uḥud behind them, where a negligible three hundred and thirteen ill-equipped men had triumphed over a strong army of a thousand well-equipped fighters. Thinking about their own numbers and preparations that day, some of them let slip words to the effect that *today it is impossible for anyone to defeat us — once the fighting starts, the enemy will run*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes this is reported by Ḥākim and Bazzār.

That attitude — relying solely on one's own power — was disliked by Allah, the commentary says plainly, and this from a group of people so dear to Him.

Mālik ibn ʿAwf had planned well: units of his army hidden in the mountain passes, the whole force to move at the early hour of dawn in one block, each man with his family and valuables behind him, swords drawn and the sheaths broken. As the Muslims entered the valley the ambush descended on them — arrows first, then swords, and the dust kicked up by the sudden charge turning day into night. The Companions lost their foothold and started running. Ayah 25 describes it exactly: *it availed you naught, and the earth, vast as it is, was straitened for you; then you turned back in flight.*

Al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib was asked outright: "O Abū ʿAmārah! Did you run away during Hunayn and leave the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?" His answer is recorded, Ibn Kathir says, in the Two Sahihs. Hawāzin, he said, was a tribe proficient with their arrows. When the Muslims met them they attacked and Hawāzin ran; then the Muslims busied themselves with collecting the spoils; then the arrows came, and the Muslims fled. But — he insisted first, before saying any of it — *the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not run away.*

## The one who was still going forward

Every account converges on the same image. The Prophet ﷺ firm in his place on his mule Ash-Shahbāʾ — a slow animal, as Ibn Kathir notes, not suitable for fast battle moves or even for escape — leading it *towards* the enemy while his uncle al-ʿAbbās held the right-hand rope and his cousin Abū Sufyān ibn al-Ḥārith the left, both trying to hold the mule back. And his voice:

**إِلَيَّ عِبَادَ اللهِ إِلَيَّ أَنَا رَسُولُ اللهِ** — *O servants of Allah! Come back to me! I am the Messenger of Allah!*

**أَنَا النَّبِيُّ لَاكَذِبْ. أَنَا ابْنُ عَبْدِ الْمُطَّلِب** — *I am the Prophet, not lying! I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib!*

Ibn Kathir reads this as great courage in the midst of confusion, when the army had run and left him behind — and, more than courage, as tremendous trust in Allah and reliance upon Him, with sure knowledge that He would give him victory, complete what He had sent him for, and give his religion prominence above all others.

Ibn Kathir says between a hundred and eighty Companions remained with him — among them Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, al-ʿAbbās, ʿAlī, al-Faḍl ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Sufyān ibn al-Ḥārith, Ayman the son of Umm Ayman, and Usāmah ibn Zayd, and many others besides. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports three hundred, or by other accounts fewer than a hundred; even they wished he would stop advancing.

Ibn Kathir says the Prophet ﷺ commanded his uncle al-ʿAbbās, whose voice was rather loud, to call at the top of his voice; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās as the one asked to call. The cry was: **"O Companions of the Samurah tree!"** — meaning the Muhājirīn and Anṣār who had given their pledge under the tree at Ridwān — and **"O Companions of Sūrat al-Baqarah!"** He called them by their pledge and by their Qurʾan. And those who were heralded began saying, "Here we are! Here we are!" The call ran through the battlefield, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, like a power current; the men who had fled were smitten with remorse and regrouped with fresh vigour. If a man's camel would not obey him in the crush, he put on his shield, got down and ran to the Prophet's side on foot.

When a large crowd had gathered around him, he commanded them to fight in sincerity, took a handful of sand, and supplicated: **اللّهُمَّ أَنْجِزْ لِي مَا وَعَدْتَنِي** — *O Allah! Fulfil Your promise to me!* He threw the sand; it entered the eyes and mouths of the disbelievers, distracting them from the fight; and they retreated in defeat.

## "He sent down His sakīnah" (ayah 26)

*Sakīnah* Ibn Kathir renders as tranquillity and reassurance, sent down on the Messenger ﷺ and on the believers who remained with him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a fine observation about the grammar. The ayah says *upon His Messenger* **and upon** *the believers*, repeating the preposition ʿalā ("upon") instead of joining them under one. Two different gifts are meant. For the Companions whose feet had slipped in the first assault, the tranquillity was what made their feet firm again and brought the runners back. For the Prophet ﷺ and those who had stayed on the war front with firmness and determination, it meant that they could see victory close at hand. The repeated ʿalā keeps the two distinct.

**"And He sent down forces you did not see."** Ibn Kathir: this refers to angels. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a careful qualification — *you did not see* means the people at large did not see them; reports that mention some individuals seeing them should not be taken as contrary to this.

Ibn Kathir cites Imam Abū Jaʿfar ibn Jarīr aṭ-Ṭabarī, through a chain reaching a man who fought at Hunayn *on the idolaters' side*. That man said that when they met the Messenger of Allah and his Companions, the Muslims did not remain in battle more than the time it takes to milk a sheep; that his side pursued them until they ended up at the rider of the white mule; and that there they were intercepted by men with white, handsome faces who said, "Disgraced be the faces! Go back." They ran, were followed, and — in his words — that was the end for them.

**"And He punished those who disbelieved; such is the recompense of the disbelievers."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains this punishment as their subjugation at the hands of the Muslims — something witnessed openly, a worldly recompense received promptly. Mālik ibn ʿAwf ran from the battlefield, leaving his family and belongings behind, and took refuge in the fort of Ṭāʾif; the rest of his people followed him off the field; seventy of their chiefs were killed; and everything they had brought as shackles fell into Muslim hands: six thousand prisoners, twenty-four thousand camels, forty thousand goats and four thousand ūqiyah of silver. When some children received wounds at the hands of Muslim soldiers, the Prophet ﷺ took immediate notice and sternly prohibited any such thing in future.

## "Then Allah will turn in mercy to whom He wills" (ayah 27)

Twenty days after the battle, at Jiʿrānah, the rest of Hawāzin came to the Prophet ﷺ having embraced Islam, and Allah forgave them. He gave them the choice between their prisoners and the war spoils they had lost, and they chose their people. Six thousand prisoners were released. The spoils he divided among the victors — including some of the *Ṭulaqāʾ*, a hundred camels each, so that their hearts would incline towards Islam — and Mālik ibn ʿAwf, who had led the whole war against him, received the same and was appointed chief of his own people as he had been before. Mālik said a poem in which he praised the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for his generosity and his extraordinary courage. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that he became a Muslim and rose to be a major standard-bearer of Islam.

And when the defeated Hawāzin fighters in the fort of Ṭāʾif kept shooting arrows at the Muslims and the Prophet ﷺ was requested to pray for a curse to fall on them, he prayed that they be guided to the right path. Being a mercy for all the worlds, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān comments, this prayer for his enemies teaches that when Muslims fight, the intention is not to subdue the enemy but to bring them to guidance — and effort towards that objective should never be neglected.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the rulings out explicitly, saying that these lessons are the very purpose for which the events were narrated:

**Never be proud of your power or your numbers.** The way you look towards Allah and His help when you are weak and deficient is exactly how your trust must rest on nothing but His help when you are strong and well supplied. At Hunayn the Muslims had the numbers, the weapons and the supplies. What they briefly lost was that trust — and it was only unseen help from Allah that won the battle.

**Justice and restraint even towards a defeated enemy.** The war material could have been taken from the vanquished Makkans by force; instead it was borrowed and returned. The lesson, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is perfect justice, mercy and magnanimity even in dealing with enemies.

**Do not forget the hard years.** Camping deliberately, on the march to Hunayn, at the very spot where the Quraysh had resolved to excommunicate the Muslims is a discipline of gratitude: when Allah gives victory and power, the days of distress are not to be forgotten.

**Never write anyone off.** Ayah 27 instructs the Muslims not to write off disbelievers who have been defeated in war, because Allah may yet give them the ability to embrace Islam and bless them with the light of faith. The Hawāzin deputation proved it — as did Shaibah, who came to kill him, and Mālik ibn ʿAwf, who led the army against him.

**Consent must be real.** When the Prophet ﷺ asked the Companions whether they agreed of their own free will to return the prisoners, a chorus of voiced ayes from the gathering was not enough for him; he took elaborate steps to ascertain the approval of each individual before acting. Rights are that serious: a person's silence, out of awe of the crowd or shame before people, is not proof of heartfelt consent. From this the jurists ruled that it is not correct to solicit contributions — even for a religious purpose — in a way that leans on one's office, power or influence, because many gentle people will give merely to avoid embarrassment. That has no genuine free will behind it, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that what is given in that spirit carries no barakah either.

passages.title: The Sacred Mosque closed; the jizyah imposed
passages.tafsir:
**These two ayat close a door and open a frontier.** Ayah 28 belongs to the "proclamation of withdrawal" announced at the opening of this sūrah: as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, it required that treaties with the disbelievers be terminated or fulfilled within a year, after which no Mushrik should remain within the sacred precincts of the Haram.

## The year, and the announcement

Ibn Kathir places ayah 28 in the ninth year of Hijrah. That year the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent 'Ali with Abu Bakr to publicise to the idolators that no Mushrik would be allowed to perform Hajj after that year, and that no naked person would perform tawāf around the House. Ibn Kathir adds that Allah "completed this decree, made it a legislative ruling, as well as a fact of reality."

Which year is "this year of theirs"? Maʿārif reports that some commentators say Hijrah 10, but the majority prefer Hijrah 9, because the proclamation was made through Abu Bakr and 'Ali in that year's Hajj season. "Such was the dictate of justice and mercy," Maʿārif says, that the Mushriks were not ordered out all at once after the Conquest of Makkah; those holding a treaty for a specified period were left to complete it, and others were given the periods of respite available to them. Maʿārif notes a later extension — the Prophet ﷺ increased this ruling to cover the whole of the Arabian Peninsula, though it could not take effect in his lifetime; Abu Bakr remained unable to attend to it because of other pressing problems, and it was 'Umar who put it into force.

## "The polytheists are but impurity" — the word *najas*

Maʿārif notes that **innamā** at the head of the sentence is a particle of *ḥaṣr* — restriction — so the sense is "the Mushriks are but filth."

Quoting Imam Rāghib al-Isfahānī, Maʿārif explains that *najas* covers every impurity one naturally averts — what the senses perceive and what one knows through knowledge and reason. The word gathers three kinds:

1. **Real** filth, which everyone perceives as such.
2. **Legal** impurity — the states that make wuḍūʼ (ablution) or ghusl (a full bath) legally necessary: janābah, the state of major impurity that follows marital relations, and ḥayḍ and nifās.
3. **Spiritual** impurity relating to the human heart — false beliefs and evil morals.

All three, Maʿārif argues, were found in the Mushriks of that time: they did not take many genuinely impure things as impure — liquor, for example; they did not believe at all in the washings religious codes prescribe against acquired impurity; and spiritual impurities of belief and character made little sense to them. Ibn Kathir draws the mirror image: the ayah "indicates that idolators are impure and that the believers are pure" — and for the believer's side he cites what is in the Ṣaḥīḥ, that the believer does not become impure.

## Which "Sacred Mosque"?

Maʿārif points out that *al-Masjid al-Ḥarām* is generally used for the walled structure around the Bayt of Allah, but that the Qurʼān and Hadith at times use it for the sacred precincts of the whole Haram of Makkah — an area of several square miles, hemmed in by limits originally appointed by Sayyidnā Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him). Al-Jaṣṣāṣ's proof is 17:1: the words there referring to the Miʿrāj are taken in this wider sense by consensus, since the Miʿrāj began not inside what is commonly known as the Sacred Mosque but at the home of Sayyidah Umm Hāniʼ, may Allah be pleased with her. His second proof is 9:7, "Except those with whom you made a treaty near al-Masjid al-Ḥarām," where the treaty was made at Hudaibiyah — outside the Haram's limits, though close by. Ibn Kathir reports the same wider sense from 'Aṭāʼ: "All of the Sacred Area — the Haram — is considered a Masjid."

## How far does the ban reach? The scholars differ

Maʿārif frames three questions the wording leaves open: is this particular to the Sacred Mosque, or do the other mosques of the world fall under it too? Is entry banned absolutely, or only for Hajj and 'Umrah? And are the disbelievers among the People of the Book included? Since the Qurʼān is silent on these details, Maʿārif says, the Mujtahid Imams gave their rulings according to their respective ijtihād. Everything turns on *what sort of impurity is meant*: if physical filth or major legal impurity is intended, no mosque may admit it; if the spiritual filthiness of kufr and shirk is meant, the ruling may differ.

**Imam Malik and other jurists of Madinah**, may Allah have mercy on them — reported by Maʿārif from Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī — held that the Mushriks are filthy on all counts, so the injunction applies equally to all Mushriks and all mosques. Their evidence includes an executive order of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Azīz instructing the administrators of cities not to allow disbelievers to enter mosques, quoting this very verse. (Ibn Kathir preserves a related report from Imam Abu 'Amr al-Awzā'ī: 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Azīz wrote to his governors to prevent Jews and Christians from entering the mosques of the Muslims, citing the same verse.) They also cite a saying of the Prophet ﷺ that he did not make entry into the mosque lawful for a woman in menstruation or a person in the state of major impurity — and since Mushriks do not generally take the bath when in janābah, their entry is barred.

**Imam Shāfi'ī** held that the injunction applies to all Mushriks and to the disbelievers among the People of the Book, but is restricted to the Sacred Mosque; entry into other mosques is not prohibited. His proof, which Maʿārif takes from Qurṭubī, is the case of Thumāmah ibn Athāl, whom the Prophet ﷺ had tied to a pillar of his Mosque before Thumāmah embraced Islam.

**Imam Abu Ḥanīfah** read "let them not come near" in the light of the proclamation itself, whose wording was that no Mushrik would perform Hajj after that year. So the verse forbids their performing Hajj and 'Umrah in their peculiar polytheistic manner, with the exception of entering on the basis of a particular need, subject to the permission of the Muslim ʼAmīr. His supporting evidence, via al-Jaṣṣāṣ, is the deputation of Thaqīf: after the Conquest of Makkah they came to the Prophet ﷺ and he let them stay in the mosque although they were kāfirs; when the Companions said, "Yā Rasūlallāh, these are filthy people," he answered that the floor of the mosque is not affected by their impurity.

Maʿārif reads that report as making clear that the *najas* of this verse is the filth of kufr and shirk. Ibn Kathir records from 'Abdur-Razzāq that Jābir bin 'Abdullah commented on this ayah, "Unless it was a servant or one of the people of Dhimmah." And Maʿārif cites via Qurṭubī a narration from Jābir ibn 'Abdullah that the Prophet ﷺ said no Mushrik should go near the Masjid except that the person be the bondman or bondwoman of a Muslim, who could then be admitted if needed. Were outward impurity the cause, there would be nothing particular about a bondman or bondwoman; the real basis is the danger of kufr and shirk coming to dominate.

Maʿārif's summary: keeping the masājid in perfect purity has its own proofs from Qurʼān and Hadith. But *this verse* is not connected with that problem.

## "And if you fear poverty"

Ibn Kathir cites Muhammad bin Isḥāq: the people said, "Our markets will be closed, our commerce disrupted, and what we earned will vanish." Maʿārif fills in the picture — Makkah had no produce of its own, so the Hajj season was when its people found what they needed available locally.

Allah's answer is that the economic support of the entire creation rests with Him. Maʿārif addresses the phrase **in shāʼa** ("if He wills"): it does not mean there is any doubt or hesitation in carrying out the divine will. It is placed there because those whose sights are trained on material causes find such a situation hard to accept — and here the visible source of all economic support was the non-Muslims. Allah does not depend on material causes; when He intends a thing, all related causes start falling in line with His will.

Ibn Kathir shows the promise kept. Ibn Isḥāq read it as running all the way to "and feel themselves subdued": "this will be your compensation for the closed markets that you feared would result." Allah compensated the Muslims for severing ties with the idolators through the jizyah they earned from the People of the Book; Ibn Kathir notes similar statements from Ibn 'Abbās, Mujāhid, 'Ikrimah, Sa'īd bin Jubayr, Qatādah and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and others. The verse seals itself: **All-Knowing** — Ibn Kathir glosses, in what benefits you; **All-Wise** — in His orders and prohibitions.

## Ayah 29: the road to Tabūk

Ibn Kathir situates ayah 29: it was revealed with the order to fight the People of the Book, after the pagans had been defeated, the people had entered Allah's religion in large numbers, and the Arabian Peninsula had been secured under the Muslims' control. In that ninth year of Hijrah the Prophet ﷺ prepared his army to fight the Romans, called the people to Jihad, and collected an army of thirty thousand. It was a year of drought and intense heat; some people of Madinah, and some hypocrites, lagged behind. He marched toward Ash-Shām as far as Tabūk, camped about twenty days, prayed to Allah for a decision, and returned to Madinah because it was a hard year and the people were weak. Maʿārif agrees the passage is a prelude to the battle of Tabūk, reporting from Tafsīr al-Durr al-Manthūr that Mujāhid said these verses were revealed about that battle.

**Who are "the People of the Book"?** Maʿārif notes that in its literal sense the term covers every disbelieving group that believes in a Scripture, but in the terminology of the Qurʼān it is used for Jews and Christians only, since only those two groups were well known in and around Arabia — hence Allah's words addressing the Mushriks of Arabia, "lest you should say: the Book was sent down only upon two groups before us, and we were ignorant of what they studied" (6:156).

Why single them out, when the reasons the ayah gives are common to all disbelievers? Maʿārif answers that Muslims might have hesitated to fight them on the ground that they are believers in a certain degree — in the Torah and the Injīl, and in Sayyidnā Mūsā and 'Īsā (peace be upon them) — so their connection with past prophets and Books might have dissuaded them from Jihad. There is a further hint: in a certain way these people deserved greater punishment, for they were people with knowledge, whose Scriptures described the last of the Prophets ﷺ in detail, and who knew all this yet elected to reject the truth.

## Four reasons — and why their faith is denied

But Jews and Christians did profess belief in Allah and a Last Day. Why is their faith negated? Because, Maʿārif answers, mere words of faith are hardly sufficient to prove actual belief: not having the kind of faith desirable in the sight of Allah amounts to having no faith at all. They did not openly reject tawḥīd, the oneness of Allah — yet, as the next verse states, the Jews took Sayyidnā 'Uzayr and the Christians took Sayyidnā 'Īsā (peace be upon them) to be sons of Allah, assigning them partnership in His divinity, so that their confession of pure monotheism became ineffectual. Their faith in the Hereafter likewise: many held that on the Day of Qiyāmah there would be no return to life in bodily form, only a kind of spiritual life, and that Paradise and Hell were no particular places at all — spirit when happy was Paradise, spirit when gloomy was Hell. And they did not believe in the unlawfulness of much that the Torah and Injīl prohibited — ribā (interest), for instance, and a range of prohibited foods, which they indulged in freely.

From this Maʿārif draws a rule of conduct: **taking as lawful what Allah has declared unlawful is not simply the commitment of a sin — it is kufr, a flat rejection of faith itself; and taking something lawful to be unlawful is also kufr. But should someone fall short in practice while still taking the unlawful as unlawful, that is a sin, not kufr.**

Ibn Kathir adds the same point from the other side: had they been true believers in their religions, that faith would have directed them to Muhammad ﷺ, because all the Prophets gave the good news of his advent and commanded that he be obeyed. They follow the religion of earlier Prophets not because it came from Allah but because it suits their desires — so a claimed faith in an earlier Prophet will not benefit them.

## Jizyah — the end-point of the fighting

Since all wars must end, this ayah sets a limit: *until they pay the jizyah with their own hands while they are humbled*.

Maʿārif explains that *jizyah* literally means return or recompense, and in the terminology of the Sharī'ah it is the amount taken from disbelievers in lieu of killing. The reasoning: kufr and shirk are rebellion against Allah and His Messenger, for which killing is the real punishment; but in His perfect mercy Allah reduced that punishment by giving an option. Should they agree to live as subjects of the Islamic state under its general legal framework, they may remain against payment of a nominal amount — and as citizens of that state, the protection of their life, property and honour becomes the responsibility of the Islamic government, with no hindrance placed before the observance of their religious duties.

The amounts, as Maʿārif records them, were small:

- Where jizyah is fixed by mutual conciliation, the Sharī'ah imposes no prescribed limit. The Prophet ﷺ concluded a peace pact with the people of Najrān under which they agreed to give two thousand *ḥullahs* a year — a ḥullah being a pair of clothes — each valued at one ūqiyah of silver, approximately 122.472 grams.
- A similar agreement was reached between 'Umar and the Christians of Banū Taghlib, stipulating that their jizyah be levied at the rate of Zakah, but twice over.
- Where Muslims conquered land in war and left its residents in possession of their properties as law-abiding citizens, the rate 'Umar fixed and implemented in his Khilāfah was four dirhams from the rich, two from the middle class, and one from the active poor who earned by wages or by making and vending things — a monthly dirham, about 3.618 grams of silver or its equivalent.
- Nothing at all was to be taken from the very poor, the disabled and handicapped, women, children, aged people, or religious leaders living in seclusion.

Even at those rates, Maʿārif reports instructions from the Prophet ﷺ that no one should be made to pay more than he could afford, and (citing Mazharī) that if anyone oppressed a non-Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ himself would support that non-Muslim against his oppressor on the Day of Qiyāmah. Reports of this kind led some Muslim jurists to hold that the Sharī'ah fixes no particular rate at all, leaving it to the ruler of the time to determine what is appropriate to existing conditions.

Maʿārif adds: **jizyah is compensation for removing the punishment of killing, not a substitute for Islam.** The proof is the exempt categories above, who observed the precepts of their religion freely and paid nothing; had jizyah been taken in lieu of Islam, it would have been taken from them too. And although the ayah names the People of the Book, the majority of Muslim jurists hold that accepting jizyah and stopping the fighting includes all disbelievers, whether of the People of the Book or otherwise — with the Mushriks of Arabia excluded, since jizyah was not accepted from them.

## "With their own hands, while they are humbled"

The commentators weight the closing words differently. Maʿārif, following Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, parses **'an yad**: *'an* here denotes cause, and *yad* (hand) signifies power and subjugation. The payment must not be made in the spirit of a voluntary contribution or charity; it is made in recognition and acceptance of the Islamic victory and of willingness to live under it. As for **wa hum ṣāghirūn**, Maʿārif reports Imam Shāfi'ī's explanation (via Rūḥ al-Maʿānī and Mazharī) that they should subscribe to the common law of Islam and take on the responsibility of remaining obedient to it.

Ibn Kathir reads the same words as marking defeat and subservience — "disgraced, humiliated and belittled" — and concludes that Muslims are not to honour the people of Dhimmah or elevate them above Muslims. He cites a hadith recorded by Muslim from Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said not to initiate the greeting of *salām* to the Jews and Christians, and that if one meets any of them on a road, to force him to its narrowest part. He then points to the conditions 'Umar bin al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, required of the Christians — a treaty of peace with the Christians of Ash-Shām which the scholars of Hadith narrated from 'Abdur-Raḥmān bin Ghanm al-Ash'arī, in which they undertook not to erect or restore places of worship, not to admit any spy against the Muslims, and not to prevent any of their own who wished to embrace Islam, all of it "in return for safety and protection."

## Holding the passage together

The two ayat move from **purity** to **provision** to **policy**, each step resting on the one before.

passages.title: False sonship, lords beside Allah, and hoarded gold
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Allah exposes two corruptions that had entered the religion of the People of the Book — a false claim about His own nature, and a false authority set up in His place — then follows the trail down to what was driving much of it: money. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the four ayat 30–33 as one connected exposure of "how astray the learned and the devoted and the abstaining among the Jews and Christians had gone." Ayah 35, as the same tafsir puts it, spells out the detail of the "painful punishment" mentioned at the end of ayah 34.

## Ayah 30 — a claim that never gets past the tongue

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this ayah expands what was said briefly in ayah 29, that these people do not believe in Allah. Here is the proof: the Jews take ʿUzayr (Ezra) to be the son of Allah, and the Christians say the same of ʿĪsā — so their claim to faith in One Allah turns out to be false.

A necessary precision from the same tafsir: this was not the belief of all the Jews. Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani notes in a footnote that it was the belief of some Jews of Arabia, adding that the Dead Sea Scrolls have proved that some Jewish sects believed Ezra to be the son of Allah, and he closes with *wa'Llāhu aʿlam*, "and Allah knows best."

**"That is their saying with their mouths."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is blunt: they have no proof that supports their claim, "other than lies and fabrications." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two readings, both sound: they profess it openly through their own tongues, nothing secret about it; or this blasphemy remains the work of their tongues — they can give no reason or justification for it.

**يُضَاهِئُونَ — *yuḍāhi'ūn*.** Ibn Kathir glosses this word with one word: *imitating*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the sting explicit: by calling prophets sons of Allah, the Jews and Christians became the same as the disbelievers and Mushriks of past ages, who used to say that the angels — and their idols, Lāt and Manāt — were daughters of Allah.

**قَاتَلَهُمُ اللَّهُ.** Ibn ʿAbbas explained this expression as: "May Allah curse them." And *annā yu'fakūn* — "how they are deluded away from the truth!" — means, in Ibn Kathir's words, how they deviate from truth when it is apparent, exchanging it for misguidance. Ibn Kathir reads the ayah within the sūrah's command to fight: Allah the Exalted, he says, encourages the believers to fight the polytheists and the disbelieving Jews and Christians who uttered this terrible statement.

## Ayah 31 — worship you may not notice you are doing

**The two words.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *aḥbār* is the plural of *ḥibr*, a religious scholar among the Jews and Christians, while *ruhbān* is the plural of *rāhib*, someone who devotes himself to worship and abstains from a worldly role in life. Ibn Kathir cites As-Suddi, who said that the *aḥbār* are the Jewish rabbis while the *ruhbān* are the Christian monks — and Ibn Kathir affirms it from Allah's words in 5:63; he adds that the *qissīsūn*, the word used in 5:82, are their scholars.

**The moment that unlocks the ayah.** Ibn Kathir reports, from Imam Ahmad, At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Jarir At-Tabari through several chains of narration, the account of ʿAdi bin Hatim, may Allah be pleased with him, who had become a Christian during the time of Jāhiliyyah. ʿAdi came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Al-Madinah **wearing a silver cross around his neck.** The Prophet ﷺ recited this very ayah: *They took their rabbis and their monks to be their lords besides Allah.*

ʿAdi objected: "I said, 'They did not worship them.'" The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Yes they did. They (rabbis and monks) prohibited the allowed for them (Christians and Jews) and allowed the prohibited, and they obeyed them. This is how they worshipped them."

ʿAdi embraced Islam and pronounced the Testimony of Truth, and Ibn Kathir records that the face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ beamed with pleasure. He then said to ʿAdi, "Verily, the Jews have earned the anger (of Allah) and the Christians are misguided."

**Why this matters.** Ḥudhayfah bin Al-Yaman, ʿAbdullah bin ʿAbbas and several others explained the ayah exactly this way: the Christians and Jews obeyed their monks and rabbis in whatever they allowed or prohibited for them. That is why Allah follows it immediately with *while they were commanded to worship none but one Deity (ilāh)* — the One, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "whatever He renders prohibited is the prohibited, whatever He allowed is the allowed, whatever He legislates, is to be the law followed, and whatever He decides is to be adhered to."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reasons the same way. They used to call their religious leaders their Lord in clear terms; but even supposing they did not believe those leaders to be gods, they had virtually transferred to them the right to be obeyed — a right belonging to Allah absolutely and exclusively — following their dictates even where those dictates ran against Allah and His Messenger. That, says the tafsir, "is like taking someone as god — an act of flagrant blasphemy, an open kufr."

The ayah closes with *None has the right to be worshipped but He. Hallowed be He above what they associate.* Ibn Kathir: exalted, sanctified, hallowed above partners, equals, aids, rivals **or children**.

**A clarification worth having.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful that this ayah has no bearing on the familiar question of following a juristic school (*taqlīd*). Common people who are not aware of religious precepts trust the ʿulamā' and follow their fatāwā; those not competent to occupy the station of *ijtihād* (independent legal reasoning from the primary sources) follow the Mujtahid Imams. That following, says the tafsir, is in real terms nothing but following the dictates of Allah and His Messenger through those with direct access to the sources of the Sharīʿah — exactly what the Qur'an instructs: *So ask the people of knowledge if you do not know* (16:43). Usmani's footnote draws the line: one who follows an imam does not believe him to be an independent point of obedience but consults him as an interpreter of Qur'an and Sunnah, and will not follow him where his view clearly clashes with a clear-cut ruling of Qur'an and Sunnah. The case of the Jews and Christians was totally different: they believed their religious leaders to be law-givers, infallible, to be obeyed even where their rulings contradicted the scriptures.

## Ayat 32–33 — blowing at the sun

Ibn Kathir gives the image that carries ayah 32: those who try, through argument and lies, to extinguish the guidance and religion of truth that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent with are like a man who wants to extinguish the light of the sun or the moon **by blowing at them.** Such a person will never accomplish what he sought. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the escalation: in ayah 31 they followed the false and obeyed people other than Allah; in ayah 32 they compound the error by trying to black out the Faith of Truth for others.

Allah's reply is not merely that they will fail: *Allah will not allow except that His Light should be perfected, even though the disbelievers hate it.* On *kāfir*, Ibn Kathir gives the root sense: linguistically a *kāfir* is the person who covers something. The farmer is called *kāfir* because he covers seeds in the ground — and the Qur'an uses the word in that agricultural sense in 57:20, "thereof the growth is pleasing to the tillers."

In ayah 33, Ibn Kathir distinguishes the two things the Messenger ﷺ was sent with: *guidance* refers to the true narrations, beneficial faith and true religion he came with; *the religion of truth* refers to the righteous, legal deeds that bring about benefit in this life and the Hereafter.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites, as recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah made the eastern and western parts of the earth draw near for me [to see], and the rule of my Ummah will extend as far as I saw." And Imam Ahmad recorded from Tamīm Ad-Dārī that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying: "This matter (Islam) will keep spreading as far as the night and day reach, until Allah will not leave a house made of mud or hair, but will make this religion enter it, while bringing might to a mighty person (a Muslim) and humiliation to a disgraced person (who rejects Islam). Might with which Allah elevates Islam (and its people) and disgrace with which Allah humiliates disbelief (and its people)."
Maʿārif ul Qurʼān comments that this promise of Allah was fulfilled, the primacy of Islam remaining operative throughout the world for about a thousand years. The same tafsir adds a measured note from Tafsīr Maẓharī: this glad tiding of ascendancy is for most times and circumstances. Whenever Muslims acted wholeheartedly in accordance with Qur'an and Sunnah, no impediment could defeat their determination; where they reached the point of being subjugated, that was the consequence of heedlessness towards those same injunctions — while the Religion of Truth itself, in its arguments and proofs, stood its ground as always.

## Ayah 34 — the motive under the misguidance

Notice the shift: after four ayat about them, Allah addresses *the believers* — **O you who believe.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the purpose: the conduct of the rabbis and monks is described to Muslims as a warning, so that they too remain alert against such conditions arising among themselves.

Ibn Kathir makes the same point through the Salaf. Sufyan bin ʿUyaynah said: "Those among our scholars who become corrupt are similar to the Jews, while those among our worshippers who become misguided are like Christians." And Ibn Kathir cites a hadith he describes as authentic, without naming a collection: "You will follow the ways of those who were before you, step by step." They asked, "Jews and Christians?" He ﷺ said, "Who else?"

**"Many," not "all."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the word *kathīran* ("many"). Most of the rabbis and monks were involved in this practice, and under such conditions people generally tend to make a sweeping statement and call everyone bad. By saying *many*, the Qur'an prompts Muslims to mind their words even when dealing with enemies.

**"Devour people's wealth by falsehood."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies the false means concretely: giving fatwa counter to the injunction of the Torah, for money — and in doing so, on occasions, misinterpreting divine injunctions through concealment and falsification. Ibn Kathir adds the mechanism: they sell the religion in return for worldly gains, using their positions and status among people to illegally devour their property. The Jews were respected by the people of Jāhiliyyah and collected gifts, taxes and presents from them; when Allah sent His Messenger ﷺ they persisted in their misguidance, disbelief and rebellion, hoping to keep their status — and Allah extinguished all this with the light of Prophethood. As for *and hinder from the way of Allah*: Ibn Kathir says they hinder people from following the truth, confuse truth with falsehood, and pretend before their ignorant followers that they call to righteousness, when in reality they call to the Fire. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains how the damage spreads: when people see their leaders doing this, the inherent love for truth in them dies out, and basing their conduct on such false rulings they end up taking the error itself to be as good as correct.

**The third group.** With *those who hoard gold and silver*, Ibn Kathir says Allah names the third category of leadership: people rely on their scholars, their worshippers and the wealthy among them, and when these categories become corrupt, society in general becomes corrupt. He quotes Ibn Al-Mubarak: "What corrupted the religion, except kings and wicked *aḥbār* and *ruhbān*."

**What counts as *kanz* (hoarding)?** According to Malik, who narrated it from ʿAbdullah bin Dinar from Ibn ʿUmar, *kanz* refers to wealth on which Zakah has not been paid. Al-Bukhari recorded, through Az-Zuhri from Khalid bin Aslam, that ʿAbdullah bin ʿUmar said: "This was before Zakah was ordained. When Zakah was ordained, Allah made it a cleanser for wealth." ʿUmar bin ʿAbdul-ʿAzīz and ʿIrāk bin Malik said the ayah was abrogated by *Take Sadaqah from their wealth* (9:103). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues from the wording itself: *and do not spend it* indicates that those who do spend in the way of Allah as necessary are not harmed by the rest of their accumulated wealth, and cites the Prophet's ﷺ statement that wealth for which Zakah has been paid is not included under *kanaztum*, "you have accumulated" (Abu Dawud, Ahmad and others). Keeping wealth which remains after taking out Zakah is therefore no sin — the approach taken by the majority of Muslim jurists and Imams.

A fine grammatical point from the same tafsir: gold and silver are both named, yet the pronoun in *wa lā yunfiqūnahā* ("do not spend **it**") reverts to *fiḍḍah*, silver — which Tafsīr Maẓharī takes as an indicator that where a person owns a little of both, the Zakah threshold (*niṣāb*) is determined in terms of silver, the gold calculated at its price in silver.

**Not only about them.** Al-Bukhari recorded from Zayd bin Wahb that Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, said they were in Ash-Sham when he recited this ayah; Muʿawiyah said, "This Ayah is not about us, it is only about the People of the Book," and Abu Dharr replied: "Rather, it is about us and them."

## Ayah 35 — the treasure that turns on its owner

Ibn Kathir says the words that follow the branding — *This is the treasure which you hoarded for yourselves. Now taste of what you used to hoard* — will be said to them as a way of admonishing, criticising and mocking them, as in *Then pour over his head the torment of boiling water. "Taste you (this)! Verily, you were (pretending to be) the mighty, the generous!"* (44:48–49). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this a sort of verbal punishment alongside the physical one.

**Why those three places?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a striking explanation: either it means the whole body, or these three parts are precisely the parts the miser used against the poor: a miser who does not like to spend in the way of Allah would usually greet a needy visitor looking for charity or Zakah with a forehead all wrinkled with distaste; then, to avoid him, he turns away to his right or left side; and if the needy person still persists, he turns his back on him.

**The principle underneath.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it in a sentence: "The return of a deed is the deed itself." What was accumulated unlawfully — or lawfully but without paying its Zakah — becomes, by itself, the punishment. Ibn Kathir reports the same law as a saying: "He who covets a thing and prefers it to Allah's obedience, will be punished with it."

**From the Sunnah.** Imam Abu Jaʿfar Ibn Jarir recorded that Thawban said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to declare: "Whoever leaves a treasure behind (on which he did not pay the Zakah), then on the Day of Resurrection his wealth will be made like a bald-headed poisonous male snake with two black spots over the eyes. The snake will follow him, and he will say, 'Woe to you! Who are you?' The snake will say, 'I am your treasure that you left behind,' and will keep following him until the man gives it his hand; the snake will devour it and then devour his whole body." Ibn Kathir notes that Ibn Hibban also collected this hadith in his Ṣaḥīḥ, and that part of it was collected in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs from Abu Hurayrah. In his Ṣaḥīḥ, Muslim recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every man who does not pay the Zakah due on his money, then on the Day of Resurrection, his side, forehead and back will be branded with rods made of fire on a Day the length of which is fifty thousand years, until when the servants will be judged; that man will be shown his destination, either to Paradise or the Fire."

Ibn Kathir also brings a narration ʿAbdur-Razzaq recorded from ʿAli about this ayah: the Prophet ﷺ said, "Woe to gold! Woe to silver," repeating it three times. This was hard on the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said, "What type of wealth should we use?" ʿUmar said, "I will find out for you," and put the question to the Prophet ﷺ, who answered: **"A remembering tongue, an appreciative heart and a wife that helps one of you implement his religion."**

## Living it

**Guard where obedience ends.** Following scholars is not the sin — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān rules that out explicitly, and calls asking the people of knowledge obedience to Allah. The sin in ayah 31 is treating a man as an independent point of obedience.

**Watch what money does to religious knowledge.** Sufyan bin ʿUyaynah aimed the warning of ayah 34 at *our* scholars and *our* worshippers, not somebody else's.

**Pay the Zakah, and do not read ayah 34 as a verse about other people.** Abu Dharr settled that instinct: "Rather, it is about us and them." And in the words of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the return of a deed is the deed itself; the hoard becomes the punishment.

passages.title: Twelve months and the sin of intercalation
passages.tafsir:
## What these two ayat are doing

Ayah 36 states the shape of time itself: twelve months, fixed by Allah and written in His Book on the day He created the heavens and the earth, four of them sacred. Ayah 37 condemns the practice that broke that shape — *al-nasīʾ*, the pagan Arab habit of sliding a sacred month off its place and pinning its sanctity onto a different month. Together they make one argument: the order and names of the months are not terms coined by human beings, they are Allah's decree — and tampering with them is, as ayah 37 puts it, an addition to disbelief.

## The custom being dismantled

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. These two turn to another custom of the age of ignorance that Muslims are told to keep clear of.

All the religious codes of the earlier prophets accepted a year of twelve months, four of which were sacred and due great reverence: the three consecutive months of Dhū al-Qaʿdah, Dhū al-Hijjah and Muharram, and the month of Rajab. In those codes, worship in these four carried greater reward, sin in them was graver, and fighting and killing were forbidden.

The Arabs of Makkah, descendants of Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) through Ismāʿīl (peace be upon him), professed to follow Ibrāhīm's way. But fighting and killing had become their only vocation, and three months of enforced peace in a row was more than they could stomach. So — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it — they spun out excuses to suit their own motives. When Muharram arrived and they wanted war, they announced: *this year Muharram is not sacred; Safar is the sacred one instead.* Another year the convenient answer was Rabīʿ al-Awwal, or they simply declared that Safar had come early and Muharram would come later. And if a campaign had eaten ten months of the year, they would announce that this year had fourteen months, so the last four could carry the sanctity.

The number was kept; what was destroyed was the *order* and *identity* of the months.

**What it actually cost.** Once the months float free, it becomes difficult to determine which month is Ramadan, which is Shawwāl, which is Dhū al-Qaʿdah, Dhū al-Hijjah or Rajab. Every ruling anchored to a month comes loose with it: the injunctions of Hajj during the ten days of Dhū al-Hijjah, the fasting of the ten days of Muharram, the rules of Zakāh at the end of the year. As a direct result, hundreds of Islamic laws were distorted and compliance with them rendered useless.

## The moment the calendar came home

Makkah was conquered in the 8th year of the Hijrah. When the Prophet ﷺ then sent Sayyidunā Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) to proclaim the withdrawal from the disbelievers and Mushriks at the Hajj season of year 9, that month was — by genuine reckoning — Dhū al-Hijjah. But by the old Jāhilī custom it had been declared Dhū al-Qaʿdah.

Then came year 10, the Farewell Hajj. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it, nature would have it that the genuine month was Dhū al-Hijjah — and by the arbitrary reckoning of the people of Jāhiliyyah too, that year turned out to be Dhū al-Hijjah. It was on that occasion, in his address at Minā, that the Prophet ﷺ said that time had come back to its position as Allah had set it the day He created the heavens and the earth.

## The sermon itself

Imām Ahmad recorded that Abū Bakrah (may Allah be pleased with him) said that the Prophet ﷺ said in a speech during his Hajj:

> "The division of time has turned to its original form which was current when Allah created the heavens and the earth. The year is of twelve months, out of which four months are sacred: Three are in succession Dhul-Qa'dah, Dhul-Hijjah and Muharram, and (the fourth is) Rajab of (the tribe of) Mudar which comes between Jumada (Ath-Thaniyah) and Sha'ban."

He then asked them what day it was, what month, what town. Each time they answered, "Allah and His Messenger know better," and each time he kept quiet long enough that they thought he might give it another name — before confirming: the day of Nahr, the month of Dhū al-Hijjah, the Sacred Town. Then he said:

> "Verily! Your blood, property and honor are sacred to one another like the sanctity of this day of yours, in this month of yours and in this city of yours. Verily, you will meet your Lord and He will question you about your actions. Behold! Do not revert to misguidance after me by striking the necks of one another. Have I conveyed? It is incumbent upon those who are present to inform those who are absent, because those who are absent might comprehend (what I have said) better than some who are present."

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim collected this hadith.

He is standing in the very month, on the very day, in the very city whose sanctity had been shuffled around for generations — and he makes them name each one aloud. Sacred time is not an abstraction; it becomes the measure for how a Muslim treats another Muslim.

## "Rajab of Mudar"

The Arabs disagreed about which month Rajab was. Some tribes gave the name Rajab to the month we know as Ramadan; the tribe of Rabīʿah placed it between Shaʿbān and Shawwāl. The tribe of Mudar held that Rajab is the month between Jumādā (ath-Thāniyah) and Shaʿbān. By saying "Rajab of Mudar," the Prophet ﷺ attested to the custom of Mudar and closed the ambiguity.

Ibn Kathīr cites a small book by Shaykh ʿAlam ad-Dīn as-Sakhāwī, in which Sakhāwī says Muharram is so named because it is a sacred month. Ibn Kathīr then gives his own view: it was so named to *emphasise* its sacredness, precisely because the Arabs would switch it around — sacred one year, not the next.

## Why four, and why in that arrangement

Ibn Kathīr gives the wisdom of the pattern: the four sacred months were made four, three in succession and one alone, so that Hajj and ʿUmrah are performed with ease. Dhū al-Qaʿdah, the month before the Hajj month, was made sacred because they refrained from fighting during that month; Dhū al-Hijjah, the next month, because it is the month of Hajj, during which the Hajj rituals were performed; Muharram, which comes next, so that they are able to go back to their areas in safety after Hajj. Rajab sits alone in the middle of the lunar year, made sacred so that those coming from the farthest areas of Arabia are able to perform ʿUmrah and visit the House and then return to their areas safely. Sacred time here is mercy with a practical shape: a stretch of peace long enough to go and to come home again. (Ibn Kathīr notes that the Arabs of the Jāhiliyyah did consider these four sacred — except a group called *al-Basl*, who out of exaggeration in religion held eight months of the year sacred.)

## "That is the right religion — so wrong not yourselves therein"

Ibn Kathīr reads *dhālika ad-dīn al-qayyim* as the Straight Law: implementing Allah's order concerning the months He made sacred, and their true count as it was originally written by Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this covers the setting and serial order of the months too; making changes, alterations, additions or deletions is a sign of crookedness in comprehension and temperament.

On *"so wrong not yourselves therein,"* two complementary readings:

**It refers to the sacred four.** Ibn Kathīr: sin in these months is worse than sin in other months — just as sins in the Sacred City are written multiplied, as in the ayah about whoever inclines to evil actions or wrongdoing therein (22:25). Qatādah said: "Injustice during the Sacred Months is worse and graver than injustice in other months. Verily, injustice is always wrong, but Allah makes things graver than others as He will."

**It refers to all twelve.** ʿAlī ibn Abī Talhah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) that "so wrong not yourselves therein" connects back to the number of months at the start of the ayah — "In all (twelve) months. Allah then chose four out of these months and made them sacred, emphasizing their sanctity, making sinning in them greater, in addition to, multiplying rewards of righteous deeds during them."

Qatādah's wider comment: Allah has chosen some of His creation above others — Messengers from among the angels and from among men, His Speech above all speech, the Masājid above other areas of the earth, Ramadan and the sacred months above all months, Friday above the other days, and Laylat al-Qadr above all nights. "Therefore, sanctify what Allah has sanctified, for doing so is the practice of people of understanding and comprehension."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads "do not wrong yourselves therein" as covering three failures: acting against the compliance-worthy injunctions tied to these months, not observing proper respect for them, or falling short in devoting oneself to worship during them. And it cites Imām Abū Bakr al-Jassās in *Ahkām al-Qurʼān*: these blessed months have an exclusive characteristic of their own — whoever devotes himself to worship during them is awarded the ability and encouragement to engage in it during the rest of the months, and whoever makes the necessary effort to stay safe from sins in them finds staying safe during the rest of the year easier. Not making the best of these months is a terrible loss.

## Fighting in the sacred months — a genuine difference

The end of ayah 36 commands fighting the idolaters "collectively as they fight against you collectively," and here the two commentaries part company.

**Ibn Kathīr** holds that initiating battle during the sacred months is forbidden, citing 5:2, 2:194 and 9:5. What this ayah adds, he says, is permission for the believers to fight the idolaters in a sacred month if the idolaters initiate hostilities therein — as in 2:191, "And fight not with them at Al-Masjid Al-Haram, unless they (first) fight you there. But if they attack you, then kill them." He answers the obvious objection: when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ laid siege to at-Tāʾif until a sacred month started, that was a continuation of the battle against Hawāzin and their allies from Thaqīf, who had started the fighting and gathered their men for war; the siege continued for about forty days, ran several days into the sacred month, and the Messenger ﷺ then broke the siege and went back.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** takes a different line: the months were called *hurum* in two senses — fighting and killing are prohibited during them, and they are blessed months which it is obligatory to hold in due esteem and in which acts of worship become more reward-worthy — and of these two, the first was abrogated in the Sharīʿah of Islam while the second still remains operative.

What they agree on entirely is the second point: the reverence and heightened worship due in these months is binding today.

## Ayah 37: the word *nasīʾ*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word: *nasīʾ* is a verbal noun meaning to move back or postpone, and it is also used in the sense of that which is delayed (*muʾakhkhar*). That is exactly the crime — a sacred month is not abolished, it is *pushed back*. Nothing is openly denied, the count of four is scrupulously maintained, and the sanctity is simply relocated to where it causes less inconvenience.

By moving the months back and forth, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, the Mushriks of Arabia thought they would achieve two things at once: serve their material interests, and still take the credit of complying with the Divine injunction. Allah did not approve it. Their postponing was nothing but an addition to their stance of denial — Ibn Kathīr's rendering of *ziyādah fī al-kufr* is "an addition to disbelief," Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's is "an increase in the infidelity" — and it was going to lead them further astray. Ibn Kathīr frames the ayah as Allah's admonishment of the idolaters for choosing their wicked opinions over Allah's Law, allowing what Allah prohibited and prohibiting what Allah allowed, because they thought three consecutive sacred months were rather long to remain without fighting, full of anger and rage as they were.

On the phrase *"so that they may conform [only] to the number of what Allah has sanctified,"* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the ruling out plainly: a mere act of conforming to the given number cannot stand for correct compliance. The month for which the injunction has been given must be the month in which that injunction is carried out.

## The men who ran the scheme

ʿAlī ibn Abī Talhah reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that Junādah ibn ʿAwf ibn Umayyah al-Kinānī, known as Abū Thumāmah, used to attend the Hajj season every year and declare, "Abu Thumamah is never rejected nor refuted!" — treating Safar as sacred for people one year and Muharram as sacred another. Al-ʿAwfī narrated something similar from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Ibn Kathīr calls Imām Muhammad ibn Ishāq's discussion of this matter in his book of *Sīrah* very useful and beneficial. Ibn Ishāq traces the practice to its originator, *al-Qalammas* — Hudhayfah ibn ʿAbd Fuqaym, of the line of Kinānah — and down through his descendants, ending with Abū Thumāmah Junādah ibn ʿAwf, the last of them to continue the practice before Islam. The Arabs used to gather around him when Hajj finished, and he would stand and give them a speech sanctifying Rajab, Dhū al-Qaʿdah and Dhū al-Hijjah, then defer the sanctity of Muharram to Safar one year and uphold it another year, "so as to appear upholding the number (of Sacred Months) Allah made sacred. Therefore, he would allow what Allah prohibited and prohibit what Allah allowed."

It was held by one family across generations, with an annual public ceremony — a pulpit built for overriding Allah's law while looking devout. The ayah's closing words fit exactly: *The evil of their deeds is made fair-seeming to them. And Allah guides not the people who disbelieve.*

## Rulings that follow

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws these out:

**The month names and their order are not human coinage.** The day the Lord of all the worlds created the heavens and the earth, He had also settled this order and these names, and along with them the particular injunctions to be carried out during particular months. In ayah 36, *fī kitābi'llāh* — "as written in the Book of Allah" — stresses that this numerical setting of the months stood recorded in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfūz*) since eternity, while "on the day He created the heavens and the earth" indicates that although the Divine decree was promulgated in eternity, this order and setting of the months came into being when the heavens and the earth were created. (*ʿIddah* here means number; *shuhūr* is the plural of *shahr*, month. No one has the right to decrease or increase it.)

**Islamic rulings run on the lunar calendar.** In all Islamic legal injunctions, only lunar months are credible in the sight of Allah — fasting, Hajj, Zakāh and many others relate to the lunar calendar. The Qur'an also identifies the sun as a sign, "so that you may know the number of years and the count [of time]" (10:5), so keeping track of days and years through a lunar or a solar calendar is in itself equally permissible. But Allah has favoured the lunar calendar for His injunctions and made it the pivot round which the laws of the Sharīʿah revolve.

**Preserving the lunar calendar is fard al-kifāyah** — a religious obligation which, if fulfilled by some, absolves others. If the entire community of Muslims were to abandon it and forget all about it, everyone would be a sinner. If it remains viably preserved, the use of another calendar alongside it is permissible — though it is against the way of Allah and the way of the worthy forbears of Islam, so it is not good to opt for it unnecessarily.

**A limit on the prohibition.** Some have held the month intercalated to complete the count of years in other reckoning systems to be impermissible under this ayah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that is not correct: such a system of reckoning has nothing to do with the laws of the Sharīʿah of Islam. The people of Jāhiliyyah were censured for changing *religious* laws by adding to the lunar and legal months. Ordinary intercalation does not affect Islamic legal injunctions, so it is not included under this prohibition.

## Living it

**Honour what Allah has made sacred instead of negotiating with it.** The Jāhilī scheme was never open rebellion; it was a permanent search for an interpretation to suit their needs and fancies. Whenever the technical count is preserved and the substance quietly relocated, this ayah is describing us. Qatādah's rule is the antidote: sanctify what Allah has sanctified — that is what people of understanding do.

**Use the seasons Allah has favoured.** Al-Jassās's insight is a strategy, not a pious flourish. Dhū al-Qaʿdah, Dhū al-Hijjah, Muharram and Rajab arrive whether or not we notice them. And read in Ibn ʿAbbās's light, ayah 36's *so wrong not yourselves therein* is a warning about the whole year — with four months set inside it where both the loss and the gain are magnified.

passages.title: The call to march forth for Tabuk
passages.tafsir:
Maʿārif ul Qurʼān introduces these ayat as the account of an important battle — the battle of Tabuk, "almost the last battle" of the Prophet ﷺ — together with the injunctions and instructions that come with it. Ayah 40 cites the Hijrah — the Prophet's ﷺ migration from Makkah to Madinah — to stress that the Messenger of Allah has no need to depend on human help.

## The moment behind the words

Tabuk is a place close to the Syrian border, north of Madinah; Syria at that time was a province of the government controlled by Byzantine Christians. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene: the Prophet ﷺ had reached Madinah in the eighth year after the Hijrah, following the conquest of Makkah and the battle of Hunayn. Major parts of the Arabian Peninsula had come under the control of the Islamic state, and the Muslims were enjoying some peace after eight years of battles against the idolaters of Makkah.

It did not last. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān recalls that Allah had already revealed concerning the Prophet ﷺ that He would make the faith "prevail over every faith" (9:33, 48:28, 61:9) — so he and his companions would hardly have the respite to relax. Soon after they reached Madinah, Syrian traders of olive oil informed them that Hiraql (Heraclius), the Byzantine ruler, had assembled his forces at Tabuk on the Syrian border; that his soldiers had been placated by the payment of advance salaries for one year; that they had a sinister understanding with some Arab tribes; and that the plan was a surprise attack on Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ decided that their attack should be pre-empted, and that they should be challenged where they were gathered. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Tafsīr Mazharī, with reference to Muhammad ibn Yusuf Salihi.)

This Jihād was of a different order. Before, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, they had fought common people like themselves; here they were to confront the trained armed forces of Hiraql.

It was a terribly hot summer, and the people of Madinah were generally devoted to agriculture, their farms close to harvest — on this hung their economy, "rather the sustenance of the whole year." Ibn Kathir adds that this was a time "when fruits were ripe and shades tempting in the intense and terrible heat." So the Prophet ﷺ ordered all the Muslims of Madinah to come out for this Jihād, and invited some of the tribes living around Madinah to join in.

That general call, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, was two things at once: a tough test for those willing to make sacrifices for Islam, and a challenge to the hypocrites, who would have to prove their claim to be Muslims by joining or else be exposed. People reacted according to the conditions they were in, and the Qur'an enumerates them as separate groups: those strong and perfect in faith, ready without hesitation; those who hesitated at first and then joined (of both it says "who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of a group of them were about to turn crooked" — 9:117); those unable to join on the basis of a genuine excuse, whose excuse Allah announced His acceptance of (9:91); those who had no excuse to offer and simply did not go, out of sheer laziness (9:102, 9:106, 9:118 — verses that carry both admonition for their inertia and the good news that their repentance was accepted); the hypocrites, whose hypocrisy was too deep-seated to say yes to Jihād; and hypocrites who joined in order to spy and make mischief (9:47, 9:65, 9:74).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that the ayat before us "obviously relate to the fourth group."

And their number, it adds, was negligible. Thirty thousand set out — a number never seen in a Jihād before. Hearing that so large a force was coming against him, Hiraql was overtaken by awe and simply did not turn up on the battlefield; the Prophet ﷺ camped on the war front for a few days in the hope that the enemy might come, and when totally disappointed, returned to Madinah.

## Ayah 38: the heaviness, and what it reveals

Ibn Kathir heads this passage "Admonishing clinging to Life rather than rushing to perform Jihad," and explains that Allah here admonishes those who lagged behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the battle of Tabuk. The opening clause is **"What is the matter with you, that when you are asked to march forth in the cause of Allah"**.

Then comes the word for what they did instead: *iththāqaltum ilā al-arḍ*. Ibn Kathir renders it **"you cling heavily to the earth"**, and explains it as "reclining to remain in peace, shade and ripe fruits."

Then the question: **"Are you pleased with the life of this world rather than the Hereafter?"** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums it up in one line: "This was the diagnosis of the disease."

What has been said here relates to a particular event, it grants; but on reflection, "the real cause of negligence towards faith — and of every crime and sin — is nothing but this love for the material and heedlessness towards the life to come." It quotes the Prophet ﷺ as saying that the love of dunyā — the material life of this present world — is at the top of every error and sin. (The commentary names no collection for it.)

## The cure inside the same ayah

The ayah gives the remedy in its closing clause: **"But little is the enjoyment of the life of this world compared to the Hereafter."** Ibn Kathir describes the movement: "Allah next diminishes the eagerness for this worldly life and increases it for the Hereafter."

**The finger and the sea.** Imam Ahmad recorded that Al-Mustawrid, a member of Banū Fihr, said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "The life of this world, compared to the Hereafter, is just like when one of you dips his finger in the sea, let him contemplate how much of it his finger would carry." The Prophet ﷺ pointed with his index finger. Muslim collected this hadith.

**The traveller's provisions.** Ath-Thawrī narrated that Al-Aʿmash said of this ayah: "What compares to the provision a traveler takes."

**A dying man's shroud.** ʿAbdul-ʿAzīz bin Abī Hāzim narrated that his father said that when ʿAbdul-ʿAzīz bin Marwān was dying he asked for the shroud he would be covered with, so that he could inspect it. When it was placed before him he looked at it and said, "Is this what I will end up with from this life?" Then he turned his back and cried, saying, "Woe to you, O life! Your abundance is truly little, your little is short lived, we were deceived by you."

## Ayah 39: the verdict

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes ayah 39 as the verdict delivered after the notice of warning to "the lazy and the listless" about their disease and its treatment.

**"He will punish you with a painful torment."** Ibn Kathir cites Ibn ʿAbbās, who said, "Allah's Messenger ﷺ called some Arabs to mobilize, but they lagged behind and Allah withheld rain from coming down on them, and this was their torment."

**"And will replace you by another people."** Ibn Kathir explains: a people "who will give aid to His Prophet ﷺ and establish his religion." He sets beside it another ayah: "And if you turn away, He will exchange you for some other people and they will not be your likes" (47:38).

**"And you cannot harm Him at all."** Ibn Kathir: "you can never harm Allah when you lag behind and stay away from joining Jihad." And the reason the ayah closes with, **"Allah is able to do all things"**, he explains in five words: "He is able to destroy the enemies without your help."

## Ayah 40: the cave, and the proof of the point

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows how ayah 40 presses home that their refusal brings no loss to Allah: by citing the event of the Hijrah, it stresses that "the Rasul of Allah has no need to depend on any human help and support" — Allah can help him directly through unseen factors, as He did at the time when his own people had forced him to leave his homeland.

Ibn Kathir tells the episode: during the year of the Hijrah the idolaters tried to kill, imprison or expel the Prophet ﷺ, who escaped with his friend and Companion Abū Bakr bin Abī Quhāfah to the cave of Thawr. They remained there three days, until the pagans sent in pursuit returned to Makkah, and then proceeded to Madinah.
