Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the atmosphere: enemy foot soldiers and riders looking for them in hot pursuit; the hiding place no fortified fortress but just a cave, with the search party reaching close to its edges.

Inside, Abū Bakr was afraid — and both sources are careful about what he feared. Ibn Kathir: he "was afraid the pagans might discover them for fear that some harm might touch the Messenger ﷺ." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: he "was worried, not for his own safety, but about his master," while the master himself "was sitting calm like a mountain at peace." Ibn Kathir adds that the Prophet ﷺ kept reassuring him and strengthening his resolve. Imam Ahmad recorded from Anas that Abū Bakr said, "I said to the Prophet when we were in the cave, 'If any of them looks down at his feet, he will see us.'" He ﷺ replied: **"O Abū Bakr! What do you think about two, with Allah as their third?"** This is recorded in the Two Sahihs.

The Qur'an preserves his words to his companion as **"Be not sad; surely, Allah is with us."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks the reader to put the conditions of that night before their eyes and ask whether someone dependent on mere material means could be that tranquil.

**"Then Allah sent down His sakīnah upon him."** *Sakīnah* is glossed in the translation itself as calmness, tranquillity, peace. Ibn Kathir gives one explanation and reports another without deciding between them: Allah "sent His aid and triumph to His Messenger ﷺ, or they say it refers to Abu Bakr."

**"And strengthened him with forces which you saw not."** Ibn Kathir: the angels. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān allows that "these troops could be troops of angels, and of the elemental forces of the entire universe too — for they are, so to say, a virtual army of Allah."

**"And made the word of those who disbelieved the lowermost, while the Word of Allah became the uppermost."** Ibn ʿAbbās commented: "The word of those who disbelieved" is *shirk* (idolatry — the creed of the idolaters who drove the Prophet ﷺ out), while "the Word of Allah" is *lā ilāha illa'llāh*, there is no god but Allah.

Ibn Kathir brings that same phrase forward as the measure of a fighter's intention. It is recorded in the Two Sahihs that Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about a man who fights because of courage, or out of rage for his honour, or to show off — which of them is in the cause of Allah? He ﷺ said: **"He who fights so that Allah's Word is superior, then he fights in Allah's cause."**

The ayah closes on two of Allah's names. Ibn Kathir: **al-ʿAzīz**, the All-Mighty — "in His revenge and taking retribution, He is the Most Formidable," and those who seek refuge with Him and take shelter by adhering to what He instructs "are never made to suffer injustice"; and **al-Hakīm**, the All-Wise — wise "in His statements and actions."

## Ayah 41: light or heavy

**"March forth, whether you are light or heavy, and strive hard with your wealth and your lives in the cause of Allah."** Sufyān ath-Thawrī narrated from his father, from Abū ad-Duhā Muslim bin Subayh, that this ayah "was the first part to be revealed from Surah Bara'ah" — Sūrah Barā'ah being this sūrah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that in this fourth verse the command given earlier is repeated for emphasis: once the Prophet of Allah orders people to come out, they must come out as a matter of absolute obligation, "for on the compliance of this command hinges all that is good for them."

*Khifāfan wa thiqālan* — light and heavy — was filled in by the early authorities from several angles. Muʿtamir bin Sulaymān narrated that his father said Hadramī claimed he was told that some people used to declare they would gain no sin by lagging behind because they were ill or old, and that this ayah was revealed. As-Suddī glossed it: "whether you are rich, poor, strong, or weak." Ibn Kathir summarises the command as binding on the believers to march forth with the Messenger ﷺ "regardless whether they felt active, lazy, at ease or had difficult circumstances."

**Abū Talhah.** ʿAlī bin Zayd narrated that Anas said Abū Talhah commented on this ayah: "Whether you are old or young, Allah did not leave an excuse for anyone." Abū Talhah marched to Ash-Shām and fought until he was killed. In another narration, he was reciting Sūrah Barā'ah until he reached this ayah, and then said, "I see that Allah had called us to mobilize whether we are old or young. O my children! Prepare my supplies." His children said, "May Allah grant you His mercy! You conducted Jihad along with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ until he died, then with Abu Bakr until he died, then with 'Umar until he died. Let us perform Jihad in your place." He refused, and went to the sea, where he died. They could not find an island to bury him on until nine days later, during which his body did not deteriorate or change; then they buried him on the island.

**The old man of Damascus.** Ibn Jarīr reported that Hibbān bin Zayd ash-Sharʿabī narrated: they had mobilised with Safwān bin ʿAmr, governor of Hims. Among the army was an old yet active man of Damascus, his eyebrows sunk over his eyes from age, riding on his animal. "O uncle! Allah has given you an excuse," Hibbān said to him. He replied: "O my nephew! Allah has mobilized us whether we are light or heavy. Verily, those whom Allah loves, He tests them. Then to Allah is their return and eternal dwelling. Allah tests from His servants whoever thanks Him and observes patience and remembrance of Him, all the while worshipping Allah, the Exalted and Most Honored, and worshipping none else."

**What of those genuinely unable?** Ibn Kathir records As-Suddī's account: a man came forward, and he was fat, and complained and asked permission to stay behind, and the Prophet ﷺ refused; then this ayah was revealed and it became hard on the people — so, in As-Suddī's words, Allah abrogated it with "There is no blame on those who are weak or ill or who find no resources to spend, if they are sincere and true in duty to Allah and His Messenger" (9:91).

**Wealth and lives.** Ibn Kathir reads **"and strive hard with your wealth and your lives in the cause of Allah"** as Allah encouraging spending in His cause and striving with one's life seeking His pleasure and the pleasure of His Messenger ﷺ. And **"this is better for you, if you but knew"**: better, he says, "in this life and the Hereafter. You might spend small amounts, but Allah will reward you the property of your enemy in this life, as well as, the honor that He will keep for you in the Hereafter." He then cites the Prophet ﷺ as saying that Allah has promised the one who strives in His cause that if He brings death to him He will enter him into Paradise, or He will return him to his house with whatever reward and war spoils he earns. (Ibn Kathir gives this without naming a collection.)

The "if you but knew" is answered by the ayah Ibn Kathir sets beside it: "Jihad is ordained for you though you dislike it, and it may be that you dislike a thing which is good for you and that you like a thing which is bad for you. Allah knows but you do not know" (2:216). He closes with a report from Imam Ahmad: Anas said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to a man, "Embrace Islam," and the man said, "I dislike doing so." The Messenger ﷺ said, "Embrace Islam even if you dislike it."

## What the passage asks of a reader

The disease this passage names is not confined to one campaign. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names one perfect treatment: concern for the Ākhirah, the Hereafter. It places that belief among the three principles on which the articles of faith rest: *Tawhīd* (the Oneness of Allah), *Risālah* (the true mission of the messenger and prophet sent by Allah), and *Ākhirah* (the Hereafter). Of these, it says, belief in the Hereafter "is, in all reality, the moving spirit for correction of deeds and serves as an iron wall before crimes and sins." It presses the point at the modern world: material progress has reached its zenith, laws proliferate, the machinery to implement them grows — and crime increases anyway, because the disease has not been properly diagnosed and the line of treatment is not sound. The only correction it knows for that frame of mind is to remember Allah and think about the life to come; and wherever that prescription was used, it says, whole societies became models of humanity at its best — as happened in the blessed period of the Prophet ﷺ and the age of his noble Companions.

So the four ayat, read together: ayah 38 names the heaviness and prescribes an accurate measure of what this world is actually worth. Ayah 39 warns that those who will not come out face a painful punishment and replacement by another people. Ayah 40 removes the thought that the religion depends on anyone's support, by pointing at two men in a cave with Allah as their third. And ayah 41 says: march, light or heavy, with your wealth and your lives. Abū Talhah, reading that last ayah aloud as an old man, drew from it the shortest summary of it — "Allah did not leave an excuse for anyone."

passages.title: The hypocrites who begged to stay behind
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat are one sustained exposure of the men who came to the Prophet ﷺ with excuses so they would not have to march to Tabuk. A single question runs through all of them — *who asks to stay behind, and why?* — and the passage answers it by circling the same men from every side, tightening as it goes: an anonymous crowd whose loyalty has a price (42), the permission that let them hide (43), the line that separates two kinds of heart (44–45), the evidence that the excuse was empty and why their absence was a mercy (46–47), an old habit and not a sudden lapse (48), and at last a single speaker whose one sentence gives the whole game away (49).

Ibn Kathir sets the scene plainly: Allah is admonishing those who lagged behind and did not join the Prophet ﷺ for the battle of Tabuk — those who asked his permission to remain behind, falsely pretending to have legitimate reasons. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that most of the seventeen verses of this section deal with hypocrites who had, on false pretexts, secured that permission.

## The arithmetic of the reluctant (42)

"Had it been a near gain and an easy journey, they would have followed you."

The passage opens by pricing their loyalty. Ibn 'Abbas explains *ʿaraḍan qarīban* — "a near gain" — as booty right in front of them. *Safaran qāṣidan*, "an easy journey", Ibn Kathir glosses as travel for only a short distance. He then reads *but the distance was long for them* as the distance to Ash-Sham. Nothing about the truth of the call had changed; only the cost had.

**The oath they are already caught in.** "And they would swear by Allah" — Ibn Kathir specifies the timing: *when you return to them*. Their words are supplied in advance: "If we only could, we would certainly have come forth with you" — meaning, as he puts it, *had there not been a valid excuse, we would have gone out with you*. Before the army has even returned, Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ exactly what they will say and that it is false: "They destroy themselves, and Allah knows that they are liars." They will swear by the very One who has already recorded the lie.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why the plea of inability fails. Their absence was down to negligence and lethargy, and "if we only could" is unacceptable "because they did not use the ability given by Allah to pick and choose the right thing to do in His way. Therefore, the excuse of not having that ability is not valid." Pleading incapacity is itself the lie.

## The permission, and the reproach that came softly (43)

"May Allah pardon you! Why did you give them permission…"

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that 'Awn said: "Have you heard criticism softer than this, starting with forgiveness before criticism — *May Allah forgive you. Why did you grant them leave…*?" Muwarriq Al-'Ijli and others said the same.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds the same insight. Those with insight into the relationship between Allah and His Prophet ﷺ have said that he had a special attachment to Allah, such that his heart could not simply bear the shock of being subjected to questioning from Him. Had the words *why did you permit them?* come first, "the blessed heart of the Holy Prophet ﷺ would have been simply unable to take it." So the pardon is placed ahead of the question, serving two purposes: it informs him that something has occurred which Allah did not like, and it tells him in advance that he is already forgiven, so that what follows cannot break his heart. A certain displeasure does exist in the outward framework of the words — and it has been "coated with a delightful concern for sensitivities."

**On "pardon" and the Prophet's ﷺ protection from sin.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān anticipates the obvious worry: forgiveness is normally given for crimes and sins, and the Prophet ﷺ was *maʿṣūm*, protected from sin — so what is being forgiven here? The answer given is that just as there is forgiveness for sin, there can also be forgiveness for what is contrary to the preferred way (*khilāf al-awlā*) or is simply undesirable — and that does not violate the concept of the ʿiṣmah (infallibility) of a prophet.

**What the better course was.** "…until those who told the truth were manifest to you, and you had known the liars." Ibn Kathir reads *those who told the truth* as those with genuinely valid excuses, and paraphrases the divine question: *why did you not refuse them permission when they asked, so that you would know who truly obeys you, and who the liars are — those intent on remaining behind even if you did not give them permission?*

Mujahid reports that the ayah came down about people who said to one another, "Ask permission from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and whether he agrees or disagrees, remain behind!" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point: even had permission been refused, they were never going to march. What was lost was the exposure — the permission gave their hypocrisy a cover, so instead of being uncovered they went about congratulating themselves on how smartly they had deceived the Prophet ﷺ, and kept the chance to throw taunts at the Muslims. Hence Maʿārif's conclusion that the real purpose here "is not to show wrath or displeasure"; it is a way of saying that in future the motives and moves of such people should be watched and screened carefully.

**And the ruling was later relaxed.** Qatadah said that Allah criticised him as we read here, then later revealed permission for him to allow people to lag behind if he wished, in Surat An-Nur: "So if they ask your permission for some affairs of theirs, give permission to whom you will of them" [24:62]. 'Ata' Al-Khurasani said similarly.

## The line that runs through the request (44–45)

The same act — asking to be excused — is now traced back to the two hearts it can come from.

Ayah 44 gives the believers' side: those who believe in Allah and the Last Day do not ask to be excused from striving with their wealth and their lives. Ibn Kathir gives the reason in one line: *because they consider Jihad an act of worship*. Nobody asks to be excused from something they experience as a chance to worship — so when Allah called them, they obeyed and hastened to act in His obedience. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says it from the other direction: those who believe truly and staunchly do not pick an occasion like that to seek desertion for the sake of love for their lives and wealth. The ayah closes with "Allah is the All-Knower of those who have Taqwa" — and as Maʿārif puts it, He knows those who fear Him perfectly well.

Ayah 45 gives the other side: it is only those who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day who ask leave, and Ibn Kathir specifies — without a valid excuse. Two causes are named:

- **No hope of reward.** Ibn Kathir: "they do not hope for Allah's reward in the Hereafter for their good actions." Once the Hereafter is not real to a man, sacrifice is pure loss.
- **A doubting heart** — *wa-rtābat qulūbuhum*, "their hearts are in doubt", which Ibn Kathir specifies as doubt "about the validity of what you brought them." The excuse is a symptom; the doubt is the disease.

Then the closing image: *fahum fī raybihim yataraddadūn*, "so in their doubts they waver." Ibn Kathir describes it — they take one step forward and one step back, have no firm stance in anything, unsure and destroyed, "neither belonging to these nor to those." He adds the sobering principle that those whom Allah misguides will never find a way for themselves to guidance.

## Two exposures — what they never prepared, and what they would have done (46–47)

**Preparation is the proof (46).** "Had they really intended to march forth, they would have made preparation for it." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this the exposure of the falsehood: had they genuinely wished to set out, they would of necessity have made at least *some* preparation — and they made none.

**A working test for excuses.** Maʿārif draws from this a principle reaching far beyond Tabuk. An excuse is acceptable from someone who was ready to carry out orders and was then rendered helpless by some accident; this rule applies to all matters pertaining to the excusable. But a man who made no preparation, did not even make the intention when called, and only afterwards produced a reason — his excuse "will be like the excuse of sin which is worse than the sin." The examples given are exact: a man who has made all his preparations for Jumuʿah and is intending to go when an impediment suddenly stops him has a reasonable excuse, and Allah blesses him with the full reward of that worship; a man who prepared nothing and then happened upon an excuse is offering nothing but a ruse and a pretext.

Maʿārif grounds this in the night the Prophet ﷺ camped late on a journey (*lailat al-taʿrīs*). To be sure of waking for Fajr he arranged with Sayyidna Bilal (may Allah be pleased with him) that he would sit the night out and wake everybody at morning — but sleep overtook him too, and the company woke only after the sun had risen. Consoling his Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), the Prophet ﷺ said that there is no negligence in sleep; negligence occurs only when one is awake. The excuse held precisely because, as far as it was possible to do, arrangements had already been made. As Maʿārif concludes, a decision about an excuse being reasonable or unreasonable can be taken only by knowing whether preparation was made — "simply using a lot of words to make a point gets nothing done."

**"But Allah was averse to their being sent forth."** Ibn Kathir: Allah hated that they should go out with you — *fa-thabbaṭahum*, so He made them lag behind and stay away. Then "it was said to them: Sit among those who sit at home." Ibn Kathir adds a careful qualification to those words: this was "as a part of what was decreed for them" — and, in his own words, *not that He legislated that they stay behind*.

**Why their absence was a mercy (47).** Allah then explains why He disliked their marching: "Had they marched out with you, they would have added to you nothing except disorder."

- *Khabāl* — disorder. Ibn Kathir's reason: "because they are cowards and failures." Numbers are not strength if the numbers break.
- "They would have hurried about in your midst… sowing sedition among you." Ibn Kathir: they would have rushed to spread false stories, hatred and discord among you.
- "And there are some among you who would have listened to them." Ibn Kathir names the danger: some would have obeyed them, given preference to their speech and words, and asked them for advice, unaware of the true reality of these hypocrites — which might have caused corruption and great evil between the believers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it plainly: among the Muslims there were also simple people, who could be easily taken advantage of and were likely to be affected by their false rumours.

Muhammad bin Ishaq identifies the weight of the men involved: those who sought permission to lag behind included some of the chiefs, such as 'Abdullah bin Ubayy bin Salul and Al-Jadd bin Qays, who were masters of their people. Allah made them lag behind because He knew that if they went along with the Messenger ﷺ they would sow sedition in his army. There were some in the Prophet's ﷺ army who liked these chiefs and were ready to obey them, because they considered them honourable.

**"And Allah is the All-Knower of the wrongdoers."** Ibn Kathir draws a point of belief from the closing phrase: Allah knows what occurred, what will occur, and — for what never occurred — how it would have occurred had it happened. He cites parallels: "But if they were returned to the world, they would certainly revert to that which they were forbidden" [6:28]; "Had Allah known of any good in them, He would indeed have made them listen" [8:23]; and 4:66–68, where very few would have obeyed a harder command, though obeying would have been better for them and would have strengthened their conviction.

## Not a new lapse but an old habit (48)

"They had already sought to spread discord before and devised plots against you."

Ibn Kathir places it in history: for a long time these men had thought and plotted against the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, as well as attempting to extinguish his religion. It occurred soon after the migration to Al-Madinah, when the pagan Arabs joined forces and the Jews and hypocrites of Al-Madinah waged war against the Messenger ﷺ. Then Allah gave victory at Badr and raised his word high — and 'Abdullah bin Ubayy and his fellows said, "This is a matter that has prevailed," and embraced Islam outwardly. Ibn Kathir's observation: whenever Allah elevated Islam and its people in might, the hypocrites only increased in rage and disappointment. Their Islam was a calculation about which side was winning, so victory could never make them glad. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that "they sought disorder even earlier" refers to what had happened in the battle of Uhud.

**The comfort in the closing words.** "…until the truth came and the decree of Allah became manifest, though they hated it." Maʿārif reads this ending as an indication that victory is in the hands of Allah. It was proved on earlier occasions when the Prophet ﷺ was blessed with victory, and the same will happen in this campaign too, when all the tricks played by the hypocrites will fail.

## The crowd narrows to one man (49)

"There are some of them who say, 'Exempt me and do not put me to trial.'"

Muhammad bin Ishaq reported from Az-Zuhri, Yazid bin Ruwman, 'Abdullah bin Abi Bakr, 'Asim bin Qatadah and several others that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Al-Jadd bin Qays from Bani Salimah, "Would you like to fight the yellow ones (the Romans) this year?" He replied: "O Allah's Messenger! Give me permission to remain behind and do not cause Fitnah for me. By Allah! My people know that there is not a man who is more fond of women than I. I fear that if I see the women of the yellow ones, I would not be patient." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned away from him and said, "I give you permission." Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and several others that the ayah was revealed in his case; he was among the chiefs of Bani Salimah.

Look at the shape of that excuse: desertion dressed in the language of piety. Allah's answer cuts straight through: "Surely, they have fallen into trial." Ibn Kathir: they fell into it because of the statement they uttered, and the Fitnah he fell into by not joining the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, preferring his own safety to the safety of the Messenger ﷺ, is worse than the Fitnah he falsely claimed to fear. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: such people were not very smart — trying to hide behind an imaginary ordeal, they did not realise they had already fallen into a certain one, the ordeal of acting against the command of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, and of deserting the campaign, right there on the spot.

Ibn Kathir adds a report about the same man, noting that it is also recorded in the Sahih: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked, "Who is your chief, O Bani Salamah?" They said, "Al-Jadd bin Qays, although we consider him a miser." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "There is not a disease worse than stinginess! Therefore, your chief is the white young man with curly hair, Bishr bin Al-Bara' bin Ma'rur."

**"And verily, Hell is surrounding the disbelievers."** Ibn Kathir: they will never be able to avoid, avert, or escape from it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two possible meanings: either Hell will encircle them in the Hereafter, or the very chain of causes now operating to take them there, which has them encircled even now, is what is being equated with Hell — so that they happen to be, already, within the larger circle of nothing but the Fire.

## Living it

**Test your excuses by your preparation, not by your reasons.** This is Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's principle from ayah 46. Before deciding whether an obstacle excused you, ask honestly what you had arranged before it appeared. The man who prepared and was stopped has his full reward; the man who prepared nothing and then found a reason has only a reason.

**Do not sanctify your own reluctance.** Al-Jadd ibn Qays turned reluctance into a piety claim. When we decline an obligation in the language of religion — protecting ourselves from a trial we invented — ayah 49 is speaking to us: the ordeal you are avoiding may be nothing next to the one you are stepping into.

**Watch what you find easy.** Ayah 42 does not accuse them of refusing to serve; it observes that they would have served for a short trip and a quick gain. Measure your commitment where it costs, not where it pays.

**Guard your ear.** Ayah 47 puts the blame on the whisperers, but it also names *listeners* among the believers — men who admired prominent voices and were ready to obey them because they thought them honourable, unaware of what those men really were. Respect given to the wrong person is a door.

**And take the comfort of ayah 48.** Victory is in the hands of Allah; the decree of Allah becomes manifest, though they hate it.

passages.title: Their glee at misfortune answered by destiny
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat catch the hypocrites at the exact moment they give themselves away — not by what they say in public, but by how they react to what happens to the Prophet ﷺ. Ayah 50 exposes the reflex; ayah 51 gives the Prophet ﷺ the reply he is told to make, the creed that renders that reflex harmless; ayah 52 turns the whole thing around and shows that the believer's ledger has no losing column in it at all. The unit moves from *their* glee, to *our* certainty, to *their* dead end.

## Ayah 50: a heart read by its reactions

Ibn Kathir opens with the plain point: here "Allah emphasizes the enmity that the hypocrites have for the Prophet ﷺ." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why this particular test is so revealing. These people "live among Muslims giving the outward impression that they are one of them, but they are soon exposed by their inner reactions to what happens to the Holy Prophet ﷺ."

Look at the shape of the ayah. If a **ḥasanah** reaches you — Ibn Kathir glosses it as "a blessing, such as victory and triumph over the enemies," the sort of thing that pleases the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions — then *tasu'hum*: Ibn Kathir renders it "it grieves them," Maʿārif "it annoys them." And if a **muṣībah**, a calamity, reaches you, they start talking.

The Arabic uses one and the same verb for both arrivals: *tuṣibka* — the blessing "strikes" you and the calamity "strikes" you. That verb then carries straight through the passage: *lan yuṣībanā* in ayah 51 ("nothing will strike us"), *yuṣībakum* in ayah 52 ("that Allah strike you"). Nothing in these three ayat merely happens; things *land*. The only real question the passage asks is who sends them — and ayah 51 answers it.

**"We had already taken care of our problem."** Their line when bad news comes is قَدْ أَخَذْنَا أَمْرَنَا مِن قَبْلُ. Ibn Kathir unpacks it in one sentence: "they say, we took precautions when we did not join him" — i.e. we saw this coming, we kept our distance, we hedged. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: "They would take it as expedient in their favour that they did not go along with Muslims and found the results satisfying enough to go away delighted."

**And the tell is the final word.** وَيَتَوَلَّوا وَّهُمْ فَرِحُونَ — "and they turn away *rejoicing*." Not merely relieved. Escaping harm brings anyone a quiet relief; that is nature. This is something else. The community's wound has become their vindication, and being proved right feels better to them than the ummah being safe. That is the diagnostic Maʿārif is pointing at: you cannot always read a heart from its statements, but you can often read it from its inner reactions — from what makes it happy.

## Ayah 51: the reply he is told to give

Ibn Kathir says that in the face of "the perfect enmity they have towards him," "Allah directed His Prophet ﷺ to reply." The reply is not an argument about their loyalty or a rebuke of their glee. It is a statement about who runs the world.

**Notice a small grammatical shift.** In ayah 50 the address is singular: if *you* are struck, if *you* are afflicted — it is the Prophet ﷺ alone in their sights. But the answer he is told to give is plural: *lan yuṣībanā*, "nothing will ever strike **us**"; *mawlānā*, "**our** Master." He does not answer as an individual. He answers as a body — the believers stand inside the sentence with him, and the ayah widens further at its close to "the believers" as a whole.

**"Except what Allah has written for us."** The verb is *kataba*, "has written," as Maʿārif renders it: "Nothing can ever reach us except what Allah has written for us." Ibn Kathir's comment is short and total: "for we are under His control and decree." What reaches a believer was written before it arrived. Which means the hypocrite's calculation — *we kept clear and it paid* — was never the calculation he thought it was. Maʿārif's word for that whole way of reading events is unsparing: those who lean on material causes this way "were in a serious deception."

**"He is our Mawla."** Ibn Kathir glosses *Mawlā* as "Master and protector," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "our Master, Guardian and Helper." The word carries both halves at once: the One who owns and disposes, and the One who stands by you. This matters here, because a decree from a distant power would be something merely to be endured. A decree from your *Mawlā* is something else entirely: it comes from the One whose protection you are already under. Ibn Kathir closes the ayah on that note — "we trust in Him. Verily, He is sufficient for us and what an excellent guardian."

**"And in Allah let the believers put their trust."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what this is aimed at. The Prophet ﷺ is being asked to tell "those, who worship material causes such as these, that they were in a serious deception. These material causes were no more than a curtain. The power that moves inside them belongs to none but Allah." Ayah 51 does not deny that causes exist. It denies that they are the ones deciding. As Maʿārif puts it, Muslims "must see material causes as no more than effective agents and signs while never taking them to be the real dispensers of any good or evil."

## Tawakkul is not sitting down

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this ayah as the place where the twin issues of **taqdīr** (destiny) and **tawakkul** (trust in Allah) come into sharp focus — and it spends its energy on the misunderstanding, because the mistake runs in two opposite directions. Speaking generally, it notes, "people around the world are found in great confusion about the religious problem of Taqdir and Tawakkul."

Some of them, it says, "are plain irreligious. They just do not recognize the very possibility that something like that exists. They are content with material means as the deity they are comfortable with."

Others "lack proper awareness. They have turned destiny and trust into a pretext for their sloth and inertia." Maʿārif is blunt that this is no virtue: "The outcome of believing in Taqdir and Tawakkul should never be that one goes home, sits tight, does nothing and says what will be will be. This is no belief in destiny and this is no practice of trust."

**The correct order is both, in sequence.** "One should devote full personal energy and courage to put together whatever lawful material means one can arrange for — within the range of what lies in control. After this has been done, the matter should be resigned to destiny and trust." And then the caveat, in Maʿārif's own words: "one has to keep his or her sight trained toward Allah alone — for it is He who has the ultimate outcome of everything one does under His absolute power and control."

**And the timing of the revelation teaches it.** Maʿārif notes that the Prophet ﷺ "made full preparation for Jihad, after which, the revelation of this verse put an end to this cycle of excess and deficiency and showed the right way." The ayah did not come down instead of the preparation. It came down *after* it — the effort first, and then the heart told where the outcome actually lives. Maʿārif quotes the Persian saying for it: **بر توکل زانوے اشتر بہ بند** — "With Tawakkul [trust], do tie the knees of the camel."

The summary is worth keeping in the front of the mind: "means which you have the option to utilize, are nothing but blessings given by Allah Taʿālā. Not taking advantage of these means is ingratitude, even stupidity. Of course, do not give means the status they do not have and believe that results and outcomes are not subservient to these means — instead of all that, they obey the command of Allah Almighty."

## Ayah 52: two goods, and no third

Now the argument reverses. The hypocrites had been *waiting* — watching to see what would land on the Muslims. Ayah 52 takes their own word and hands it back to them four times over: *tarabbaṣūn* (you wait), *natarabbaṣu* (we wait), *fa-tarabbaṣū* (so wait!), *mutarabbiṣūn* (we too are waiting). Both sides are standing at the same window. Only the view differs.

**"Except one of the two best things."** إِحْدَى الْحُسْنَيَيْنِ is a dual — literally *one of the two best-things*. Ibn Kathir gives the meaning as "martyrdom or victory over you," reporting this "according to the meaning given by Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, and others." Maʿārif renders the pair the same way: "the two good things [martyrdom and victory]."

Read that carefully. The word covering both outcomes is *ḥusnā*, "the best." The believer's two possible results are not *win* and *lose*, nor even *good* and *acceptable*. Death in Allah's path and victory in Allah's path are both filed under the same superlative. Whatever the hypocrites are hoping to see is not on the list, because there is no third column for them to hope for.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes exactly this the answer to their glee: "the thing that hypocrites take as suffering for Muslims and which makes them happy is really no suffering for them. In fact, it is another form of comfort and success," because "a man of true faith becomes deserving of eternal returns and rewards even after having failed in his strong resolve, something that is the real objective of all his successes." Its conclusion is one of the finest lines in the passage: **"Therefore, he succeeds, even in failure and gains, even in loss."**

**What the believers are waiting for, on their side.** أَن يُصِيبَكُمُ اللَّهُ بِعَذَابٍ مِّنْ عِندِهِ أَوْ بِأَيْدِينَا — "either that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Himself or at our hands." Ibn Kathir explains "at our hands" as "either capture or killing." So their two possibilities are the mirror image of ours: not two goods but two forms of punishment, one direct from Allah, one delivered through the believers.

Maʿārif spells out how tightly that closes: "Either, they would be punished at the hands of Muslims right here in this world, in which case, they will taste the punishment in the mortal and the eternal world both. And, in case, they somehow escaped unscathed in the mortal world, there is no possibility of deliverance from the punishment of the Hereafter." Escaping in this life is not an exit; it only removes one of the two instalments.

**"So wait — we too are waiting with you."** The ayah ends without threat or argument. It simply lets time be the judge, and the confidence in that closing line is the whole point: a man who knows both of his outcomes are called *the best* can afford to be patient.

## Living it

**Watch what gladdens you.** Ayah 50 does not test people by their words but by their reflex when someone else's affair goes well or badly. Secret satisfaction at another believer's setback — that the thing you warned against went wrong, that you were proved right — is the very reflex being exposed here.

**Refuse the hedge.** The hypocrite's phrase, "we took our precaution beforehand," is the voice of the person who never fully commits so that he can never fully lose. Ayah 51 dismantles it: nothing reaches you but what was already written, so the hedge bought nothing.

**Work fully, then hand it over.** Tie the camel *and* trust. Take every lawful means — Maʿārif calls neglecting them ingratitude and even stupidity — and then refuse to let those means become the thing you actually rely on. They are the curtain; Allah is the power moving behind it.

**Reprice loss.** If both of your outcomes are *ḥusnā*, then the worst that hostility can do to you is deliver one of the two things you wanted. That, not bravado, is the source of the believer's steadiness in this passage.

Held together, the three ayat make one point from three directions. Events do not arrive at random and they are not steered by the clever positioning of men. The passage does not promise the believer an easy road; it tells him Whose writing decides what reaches him, and Who is his *Mawlā* when it does.
